subject: History
description: Three RTCs (1930-32), participants, Communal Award, Poona Pact, Gandhi-Irwin Pact

questions.stem: The First Round Table Conference was held in:
questions.explanation: First RTC — 12 November 1930 to 19 January 1931, at St James's Palace, London. Inaugurated by King George V; presided over by PM Ramsay MacDonald. INC boycotted (Civil Disobedience movement was in progress; key leaders arrested). Attended by Muslim League (Aga Khan, Jinnah), Hindu Mahasabha (Moonje), princely-state representatives, B.R. Ambedkar (representing Depressed Classes). No major decisions because Congress was absent.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Mahatma Gandhi attended only the Second Round Table Conference (Sep-Dec 1931). He went as the sole representative of:
questions.explanation: Following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931), which suspended Civil Disobedience, Gandhi attended Second RTC as the lone Congress representative. He arrived in London 12 Sep 1931. The conference deadlocked over the question of separate electorates for minorities (Ambedkar pushed for Depressed Classes; Gandhi opposed). Gandhi returned 28 Dec 1931 empty-handed. Civil Disobedience resumed January 1932.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 'Communal Award' announced in 1932 by British PM Ramsay MacDonald provided separate electorates for:

options.option_text: Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans AND Depressed Classes

questions.explanation: Communal Award — 16 August 1932 — extended separate electorates already given to Muslims (1909) to additional minorities, including the Depressed Classes (Dalits). Gandhi began a fast-unto-death at Yerwada Jail on 20 Sep 1932 against separate electorates for Dalits, fearing it would split Hindu society. The fast led to the Poona Pact (24 Sep 1932) — Ambedkar agreed to joint electorates with reserved seats (148 reserved instead of 71 separate).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Third Round Table Conference (Nov-Dec 1932) is most notable for:

options.option_text: Both INC AND Labour Party (UK) boycott — sparsely attended; led to White Paper March 1933
Adoption of Government of India Act 1919

questions.explanation: Third RTC — 17 Nov to 24 Dec 1932 — attended by only 46 delegates. Congress boycotted (Gandhi back in jail), and the British Labour Party also stayed away in protest at the Conservative-led government's repressive policies. Discussions led to the White Paper (March 1933), which became the basis for the Government of India Act, 1935 — provincial autonomy + federal scheme that never came into being.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact, which paved the way for Gandhi's attendance at the Second RTC, was signed in:
questions.explanation: Signed 5 March 1931 in New Delhi between Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin. Terms: Congress suspended Civil Disobedience; British released most political prisoners (except those guilty of violence), withdrew ordinances, allowed peaceful picketing, returned confiscated lands not yet sold. Quid pro quo — Gandhi to attend Second RTC. Sometimes called the 'Delhi Pact'. The Karachi Session of INC (March 1931, presided by Sardar Patel) endorsed it.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Poona Pact (1932) signed between Gandhi and Ambedkar replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with:
questions.explanation: Poona Pact (24 September 1932) — Gandhi (fasting since 20 Sep) and Ambedkar negotiated. Outcome: 148 reserved seats for Depressed Classes (up from 71 separate seats in the Communal Award) within a JOINT electorate, where all voters elect — but only Dalit candidates contest the reserved seats. This established the principle of reservation in Indian politics; carried forward into the Constitution (Articles 330, 332) for SC seats in Lok Sabha + State Assemblies.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Who chaired/presided over all three Round Table Conferences as the head of the British Government?
questions.explanation: Ramsay MacDonald (Labour Party) — British PM 1929-31 (minority Labour) and 1931-35 (National Government coalition). He inaugurated and presided over all three RTCs. The 'Communal Award' (16 Aug 1932) was issued under his name. Lord Irwin (Halifax) was Viceroy 1926-31 — Indian-side counterpart to MacDonald, signed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. Lord Willingdon was Viceroy by the Second RTC.
